faq.a: Assess pain on passive stretch of the involved muscles and check for tense, firm swelling; if present, arrange urgent fasciotomy.
faq.q: What is the first bedside test for suspected compartment syndrome?

faq.a: It causes a Trendelenburg gait—pelvis drops on the opposite side during single‑leg stance.
faq.q: How does gluteus medius weakness affect gait?

faq.a: Elevated CK identifies rhabdomyolysis, prompting aggressive IV fluids to prevent acute kidney injury.
faq.q: Why is CK measurement important in malaria patients with muscle pain?

exam: A 25‑year‑old with sickle‑cell disease presents with painful swelling of the calf; what is your differential and immediate management? — Consider compartment syndrome, vaso‑occlusive crisis, DVT; assess compartment pressure, start analgesia, hydrate, arrange fasciotomy if pressure high.

A patient cannot dorsiflex the foot but has normal plantarflexion; which nerve is injured and what muscles are affected? — Common peroneal nerve; tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, peroneus longus; look for foot drop.
During a trauma exam you find a tense posterior thigh; what condition does this suggest and what is the definitive treatment? — Posterior compartment syndrome; emergent fasciotomy.

Explain how HIV‑related peripheral neuropathy can present with lower‑limb muscle weakness. — Distal symmetric polyneuropathy affecting peroneal and tibial nerves; leads to foot drop and gait instability.
A farmer with malaria reports dark urine and calf pain; what labs and management steps are required? — Check serum CK, renal function; start aggressive IV fluids, monitor electrolytes, treat malaria.

Describe the gait change seen with gluteus maximus weakness and its clinical significance. — Lumbar hyperextension and difficulty rising from sitting; indicates hip extensor insufficiency, often from nerve injury or disuse.

What is the significance of a positive Trendelenburg sign and how do you test it? — Indicates gluteus medius insufficiency; ask patient to stand on one leg and observe pelvic drop on the opposite side.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops calf swelling; how do you differentiate drug‑induced myopathy from compartment syndrome? — Review medication history, check CK (high in myopathy), assess pain on passive stretch and compartment firmness; urgent fasciotomy only if compartment syndrome confirmed.
ai.title: Muscles of the Lower Limb
related: Peripheral nerve injuries of the lower limb
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: A systematic approach to the lower‑limb muscles links anatomy to common clinical problems in low‑resource settings. Learn functional groups, key exam findings and how muscle pathology presents.

b: Anterior compartment: dorsiflexors, knee extensors (e.g., tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, quadriceps).
Posterior compartment (superficial): plantarflexors, knee flexors (e.g., gastrocnemius, soleus, tibial posterior).
Posterior compartment (deep): toe flexors, invertors (e.g., flexor hallucis longus).
Medial compartment: hip adductors (e.g., adductor longus, gracilis).
Gluteal region: hip extensors, abductors, external rotators (e.g., gluteus maximus, medius, minimus).
sections.p: The lower limb is divided into functional compartments: anterior, posterior (superficial and deep), medial, and gluteal. Each compartment contains muscles with a common nerve supply and blood supply, allowing focused clinical assessment.

b: Femoral nerve → anterior compartment; sciatic nerve → posterior compartments.
Popliteal artery branches supply the posterior compartment; compromise causes calf muscle necrosis.
Compartment syndrome: pressure >30 mm Hg threatens perfusion; urgent fasciotomy needed.
sections.p: Understanding nerve‑muscle relationships guides localisation of neuropathies and trauma. Vascular supply predicts patterns of ischemic injury, especially in sickle‑cell disease or peripheral arterial disease common in East Africa.

b: Peripheral neuropathy (e.g., HIV‑related) → selective weakness in nerve‑supplied compartments.
Malaria‑induced rhabdomyolysis → diffuse calf pain, dark urine; risk of acute kidney injury.
Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis → painful swelling of calf or thigh muscles.
Traumatic compartment syndrome after road‑traffic injury → pain out of proportion, tense calf.
sections.p: Muscle problems present as weakness, pain, swelling or contracture. In low‑resource hospitals, bedside testing and simple imaging replace advanced studies.

t.b: Which muscle groups are weak? → Grading 0‑5 identifies nerve level and guides further work‑up.
Is pressure >30 mm Hg? → Confirms compartment syndrome; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs.
Is CK >5 000 U/L? → Indicates rhabdomyolysis; initiate aggressive hydration.

b: Ask the student to localise weakness to a nerve (e.g., foot drop → common peroneal nerve).
Present a patient with calf swelling; expect discussion of compartment syndrome vs. deep vein thrombosis.
Require description of how gluteus medius weakness leads to Trendelenburg gait.
sections.p: Examiners test integration of anatomy with bedside reasoning.

b: Attributing calf pain to gastrocnemius strain without checking for tense compartments.
Missing sciatic nerve injury by focusing only on ankle dorsiflexion.
Assuming all leg swelling is DVT; overlook rhabdomyolysis or cellulitis.
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from confusing compartments or ignoring vascular supply.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe, rapidly increasing calf pain with tense swelling (suspect compartment syndrome).
Dark urine and CK >5 000 U/L (risk of renal failure).
Progressive weakness with sensory loss suggesting spinal cord or major nerve compression.
